draftedBy: manual: Claude (claude-opus-5-5) from the two ritvikmath transcripts and the C2 goals; no API key yet, so `pnpm content draft` was not run

goals.text: Calculate the expected regret of greedy and ε-greedy after a given number of rounds, including the regret greedy incurs by locking onto a worse arm, with the correct result.
Compare how ε-greedy and UCB1 decide when to explore and say which has lower regret over many rounds, justified by how the UCB1 bonus changes with pulls and rounds.
Design a bandit model for a new decision problem, naming its arms, reward and number of rounds, and justify a choice between ε-greedy and UCB1 after checking the model's assumptions.

facts.ask: So what do I actually choose between each time, and how many times do I get to choose?
facts.text: You repeatedly choose one of several options, called arms, for example which of three restaurants to eat at every night for 300 days.

facts.ask: Do I know in advance how good each option is, or what I'll get when I pick it?
facts.text: Each arm gives a random reward from its own distribution, and these distributions and their averages are hidden at the start.
The goal is to collect as much total reward as possible over all the rounds, not only to find out which arm is best.

misconception.says: So this is basically full reinforcement learning, where what I pick changes the situation I'm in next?
misconception.truth: In a bandit, choices don't change the situation: there are no states. Only the information you gather carries over.

probes.open: So what exactly is the problem we're solving here? What do I get to choose each time?
probes.why: Why can't I just figure out which arm is best before I start?
probes.whatIf: What if there were 100 restaurants instead of 3, would it still be the same kind of problem?
probes.compute: If restaurant 1 averages 10 happiness and I eat there all 300 days, how much happiness do I expect in total?

facts.ask: When I pick one option, do I also find out what the others would have given me?
facts.text: After each choice you only see the reward of the arm you picked, not what the other arms would have given.

facts.ask: So how can I find out how good an option really is?
facts.text: So the only way to learn how good an arm is, is to try it, which is why learning about the arms costs rounds.

probes.open: When I eat at one restaurant, do I find out anything about the other ones that night?
probes.why: Why can't I learn about all the arms at the same time?
probes.whatIf: What if I could see what every arm would have paid each round, would I still need to try the worse ones?
probes.compute: With 3 arms and 30 rounds, if I try them equally often, how many rewards do I see from each arm?

facts.ask: How do I put a number on how good an option seems so far?
facts.text: An arm's value is estimated by the average (mean) of the rewards it has given so far.

facts.ask: Can I trust that number after only one or two tries?
facts.text: The estimate changes every time the arm is tried, and estimates from only a few tries can be far from the true average.

probes.open: How do I even keep track of which arm seems better so far?
probes.why: Why is the average the right thing to look at, and not just the last reward?
probes.whatIf: What if the best restaurant gave me a really bad meal on my first visit, just by bad luck?
probes.compute: An arm gave rewards 2, 9 and 4. What's my estimate for it?

facts.ask: If I get one new reward, how do I update that number without redoing everything?
facts.text: The average can be updated from the old one: new estimate = old estimate + (reward − old estimate) / n, where n is how many times that arm has been tried.
So you only need to store the current average and the count for each arm, not every past reward.

probes.open: Do I have to write down every single reward to keep my averages up to date?
probes.why: Why does one new reward move the estimate less the more times I've tried the arm?
probes.whatIf: What if the new reward is exactly equal to my current estimate, does the estimate change?
probes.compute: My estimate is 0.5 after 4 pulls and the fifth pull pays 1. What is the new estimate?

facts.ask: Once I have those numbers, what's the simplest rule for choosing?
facts.text: Greedy (exploit only) always picks the arm with the best average so far, for example after trying each restaurant once.

facts.ask: With that rule, would I ever go back to an option that looked bad early on?
facts.text: Greedy never tries an arm on purpose to learn more, so arms that looked bad early are never tried again.

misconception.says: Isn't always picking the one that looks best just the smartest thing to do?
misconception.truth: Early estimates are noisy. Greedy can lock onto a worse arm because it never collects the data that would correct the estimate.

probes.open: Once I have some averages, what's the most obvious way to choose?
probes.why: Why would I ever pull an arm that looks worse?
probes.whatIf: What if two arms are tied on their average, what does this rule do?
probes.compute: My averages so far are 7, 8 and 5. Which arm does greedy pick next, and when does it pick the 5 one again?

facts.ask: What could go wrong with greedy if the best option happens to give a bad result the first time?
facts.text: Because greedy only goes back to the current best, one unlucky early reward from the truly best arm can hide it for the rest of the game.

facts.ask: Can you show me with the restaurants how that could actually happen?
facts.text: Example: if restaurant 1 (mean 10) happens to give 7 on day one and restaurant 2 (mean 8) gives 8, exploit only eats at restaurant 2 for the remaining 297 days.
Being stuck costs the gap between the two arms' averages on every remaining round.

probes.open: Could greedy ever get it wrong and never notice?
probes.why: Why wouldn't greedy just try the other arm again later?
probes.whatIf: What if the best arm had paid really well on its first try instead?
probes.compute: If restaurant 2 averages 8 and restaurant 1 averages 10, and I'm stuck at restaurant 2 for 297 days, how much happiness do I miss out on?

facts.ask: Is there a way to mostly pick the best one but still try the others now and then? How would that work?
facts.text: ε-greedy picks a random arm with a small probability ε (for example 10%) and otherwise picks the arm with the best average so far.

facts.ask: When it does try something else, how does it decide which one to try?
facts.text: Its random picks ignore the estimates, so it spends as many of them on arms already known to be bad as on arms it knows little about.
With 3 arms and ε = 0.1, the arm that currently looks best is picked with probability 0.9 + 0.1/3 ≈ 0.93.

misconception.says: So when it picks randomly, it goes for the arms it's least sure about, right?
misconception.truth: No: ε-greedy picks uniformly at random, regardless of how uncertain each arm is.

probes.open: Is there a way to keep using my best guess but still try the others sometimes?
probes.why: Why pick a random arm instead of the one I know least about?
probes.whatIf: What if ε were 0, or 1? What would happen then?
probes.compute: With 3 arms and ε = 0.1, how likely is it that I pick the arm that currently looks best?

facts.ask: Is there a name for trying options to learn about them, versus sticking with my favourite?
facts.text: Exploration means trying arms to learn about them; exploitation means picking the best arm you know of to collect reward.

facts.ask: What goes wrong if I try new things too rarely, or too often?
facts.text: Too little exploration risks locking onto a worse arm; too much exploration wastes rounds on arms you already know are worse.
How much exploration pays off depends on how far apart and how noisy the arms are, and on how many rounds are left.

misconception.says: So exploring more is always the safe choice?
misconception.truth: Every exploratory pull of a worse arm costs reward; with a constant ε that cost keeps growing.

probes.open: It feels like I'm always torn between trying new places and going back to my favourite. Is that a real problem?
probes.why: Why not just try everything a lot at the start and then decide?
probes.whatIf: What if I only had 5 days in town instead of 300?
probes.compute: If I explore on 10% of 300 days by picking one of 3 restaurants at random, about how many days do I spend at the worst one because of exploring?

facts.ask: How do I measure how much a way of choosing costs me compared with the ideal?
facts.text: Regret is the reward you would expect from always picking the best arm minus the reward your strategy is expected to get.

facts.ask: Can you work that out with numbers, like for picking a random restaurant every night?
facts.text: Example: always eating at restaurant 1 gives 10 × 300 = 3000; picking a random restaurant every night gives 2300 on average, so its regret is 700.
Regret measures the cost of the decisions in expectation, not bad luck on individual rewards.

misconception.says: So that's just a measure of how unlucky I was with my meals?
misconception.truth: Regret compares expected rewards of the choices made with always choosing the best arm; noise in individual rewards doesn't count.

probes.open: How would I even measure how good or bad a way of choosing is?
probes.why: Why compare against always picking the best arm, and not against my own average?
probes.whatIf: What if I knew all the averages from day one, what would my regret be?
probes.compute: The best arm has mean 0.8. Over 100 rounds I pull it 60 times and an arm with mean 0.5 40 times. What's my regret?

facts.ask: Does that rule with the random picks ever stop paying for them?
facts.text: With a constant ε, ε-greedy keeps making random picks at the same rate forever, so it keeps paying for pulls of worse arms.

facts.ask: So how does that cost add up as the days go on?
facts.text: So its regret keeps growing in proportion to the number of rounds, roughly ε times the average gap to the best arm on every round.

probes.open: If I keep using the rule with the random picks for years, do those random picks ever stop costing me?
probes.why: Why doesn't ε-greedy stop picking randomly once it's pretty sure?
probes.whatIf: What if ε got smaller every day?
probes.compute: Three arms with means 10, 8 and 5, and ε = 0.1. Roughly how much regret do the random picks alone add per day?

facts.ask: Is there a smarter way to score each option, instead of picking at random? How is the score made?
facts.text: UCB1 picks the arm with the highest score: its average plus a bonus √(2 ln t / n), where t is the current round (day) and n is the number of times that arm was tried.

facts.ask: Why would that score favour options I've hardly tried?
facts.text: The average is the exploitation part and the bonus is the exploration part: arms tried only a few times get the benefit of the doubt.
UCB1 is deterministic: with the same history it always picks the same arm.

misconception.says: So UCB sometimes just picks an arm at random to try it out?
misconception.truth: No. UCB1 is deterministic; it explores by adding a bonus to arms it has tried few times.

probes.open: Is there a smarter way to pick which place to try than rolling a die?
probes.why: Why add something to the average instead of just using the average?
probes.whatIf: What if two arms have the same average but one was tried 100 times and the other once?
probes.compute: After 10 rounds, arm A was tried 5 times with average 0.6 and arm B 3 times with average 0.7. Which does UCB1 pick? (ln 10 ≈ 2.3)

facts.ask: What happens to an option's bonus each time I try it?
facts.text: Each time an arm is tried its n goes up, so its bonus shrinks and it becomes less likely to be picked just to learn more about it.

facts.ask: Could an option I haven't tried for ages ever get picked again?
facts.text: The ln t on top grows slowly with every round, so an arm that has been ignored for a long time eventually gets tried again.

probes.open: What happens to an arm's chances right after I finally try it again?
probes.why: Why does trying an arm make it less likely to be chosen the next day?
probes.whatIf: What if I never pick an arm for a very long time, does it get forgotten?
probes.compute: An arm tried 4 times at a round where ln t = 2 has bonus √(2 × 2/4) = 1. What's its bonus after 16 tries at the same round?

facts.ask: How does the regret of the bonus rule grow over a very long time?
facts.text: Because UCB1's exploration fades as its estimates become reliable, its regret grows only logarithmically with the number of rounds.

facts.ask: Over many rounds, which ends up with less regret: ε-greedy or UCB?
facts.text: So over many rounds UCB1 ends up with lower regret than ε-greedy with a constant ε, whose regret grows linearly; UCB1 is a zero-regret strategy.

probes.open: So which of the two rules ends up costing me less if I live in this town for years?
probes.why: Why does UCB's extra cost stop piling up the way ε-greedy's does?
probes.whatIf: What if I only had 20 days, would UCB still come out ahead?
probes.compute: If regret grows like 10 × ln T, how much regret is there at T = 100 and at T = 10,000? (ln 100 ≈ 4.6, ln 10,000 ≈ 9.2)

facts.ask: Does any of this break if a restaurant gets better or worse over the year?
facts.text: The model assumes each arm's reward distribution stays the same over time.

facts.ask: Does picking an option change how good it will be next time?
facts.text: It also assumes your choices don't change the situation: there is no state, only the information you gather carries over.
The usual analysis assumes the number of rounds is very large compared with the number of arms.

misconception.says: So the plain average of everything I've seen is always the right estimate?
misconception.truth: Only if the rewards don't drift. If they change over time, recent rewards should count more.

probes.open: Are there situations where this whole way of thinking wouldn't work?
probes.why: Why does it matter whether a restaurant's food changes over the year?
probes.whatIf: What if eating at a restaurant changed how good it is the next time?
probes.compute: Restaurant 1 averaged 10 for 200 days, then a new chef makes it 4. If I ate there every day for 300 days, what does my plain average say?

facts.ask: If I stayed for years, what should happen to the regret per day of a good strategy?
facts.text: A zero-regret strategy is one where the regret divided by the number of rounds goes to zero as the rounds go on.

facts.ask: Is it okay for a strategy to lose a lot at the very start?
facts.text: It may lose a lot at first, but eventually it figures out the best arm, so its regret stops growing much.
Exploring only can't be zero-regret, because it never uses what it has learned.

probes.open: If I moved to the town for good, how would I judge a way of choosing over many years?
probes.why: Why divide the regret by the number of days?
probes.whatIf: What if a strategy's regret kept going up by 1 every single day forever?
probes.compute: A strategy has regret 100 after 1,000 days and 120 after 100,000 days. What is its regret per day at each point?

facts.ask: How much should I trust an average from one visit compared with one from a hundred?
facts.text: An average based on one visit is much less reliable than one based on a hundred visits.

facts.ask: If two options have about the same average, does it matter how many times I tried each?
facts.text: So comparing averages alone ignores how many samples each is based on: 2.9 from 1 visit could really be higher than 3 from 100 visits.

probes.open: If two places have almost the same average, is there anything else I should look at before choosing?
probes.why: Why is one visit not enough to trust an average?
probes.whatIf: What if one place averaged 2.9 from a single visit and the other 3 from 100 visits?
probes.compute: One restaurant: 1 visit, average 2.9. Another: 100 visits, average 3. Which has the higher average, and which estimate could be further off?

facts.ask: Is one strategy always the best, or does it depend on the situation?
facts.text: Which strategy is best depends on the situation: how noisy the arms are, how many arms there are, and how many rounds you have.

facts.ask: When could trying each option once and then sticking with the best actually work well?
facts.text: With narrow, well-separated distributions, trying each arm once and then sticking with the best can beat UCB1, because one sample already tells you enough.

facts.ask: What if there are lots of options but only a few rounds?
facts.text: With many arms and few rounds (100 restaurants, 300 days), UCB1 has no time left to profit from exploring; it does best when rounds are many compared with arms.

probes.open: Is UCB always the right choice, or does it depend on the situation?
probes.why: Why would trying each place just once ever be enough?
probes.whatIf: What if the town had 100 restaurants and I stayed only 300 days?
probes.compute: 100 restaurants and 300 days: if UCB1 first tries each restaurant once, how many days are left, and how many more visits does each restaurant get on average?

facts.ask: Is there another way to decide when to try the less certain options, besides adding a bonus?
facts.text: Thompson sampling keeps a probability distribution over each arm's mean and picks the arm whose random draw from that distribution is highest.

facts.ask: How is that different from the bonus approach?
facts.text: It explores through randomness that shrinks as the distributions narrow, while UCB1 adds a deterministic bonus.

probes.open: Is adding a bonus the only clever way to decide which place to try?
probes.why: Why would picking by a random draw still favour the best arm most of the time?
probes.whatIf: What if I've tried an arm thousands of times, how random is its draw then?
probes.compute: Two arms: one I'm very sure has mean 0.6, one I've barely tried with a guess around 0.5 but wide. Which could still be picked sometimes, and why?

facts.ask: What if an option slowly gets better or worse over time, can my averages keep up?
facts.text: If rewards drift over time, a plain average reacts too slowly, because old rewards count as much as new ones.

facts.ask: How could I make my numbers follow those changes?
facts.text: A constant step size, new = old + α (reward − old), weights recent rewards more and lets the estimate follow the change.

probes.open: What if a restaurant slowly gets better or worse over the year, can my averages keep up?
probes.why: Why would giving recent meals more weight help?
probes.whatIf: What if α were 1, what would the estimate be?
probes.compute: My estimate is 8, α = 0.5, and tonight's meal is 4. What is the new estimate?
